meta.title: Global Crude Flow Intelligence Dashboard
meta.week_convention: Weeks run Monday-Sunday; week_ending is always the Sunday, with data captured up to the 09:00 Europe/Nicosia (Cyprus time) cutoff that Sunday morning.
meta.note: Built from free/public sources (EIA, IEA, OPEC, operator statements, Reuters/Al Jazeera/Bloomberg/OilPrice/Argus/Kpler-cited reporting) plus a seed route database. No live Kpler/Vortexa feed is connected in this build; flow figures are research snapshots, not real-time AIS-derived data. See each item's confidence tag and source.

weekly_flows.event_explanation: Pipeline shut down 13 Sep 2026 after a drone attack hit two points near Riyadh and Medina; drones traced to Maysan province, Iraq (Iranian-aligned militants). This was Saudi Arabia's primary Hormuz-bypass route (~5 mb/d recent flow, ~7 mb/d nameplate), so the shutdown compounds the ongoing Hormuz crisis rather than relieving it. Restart timeline has now firmed up somewhat: Bloomberg (16 Sep 2026) reports Saudi Arabia is seeking to restore roughly half the pipeline's capacity within days, with full capacity targeted in about six weeks. This narrows the earlier gap between Reuters' 5-6 week estimate and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright's 'within days' comment — both were partially right, referring to partial vs full restoration. Satellite imagery reviewed by analysts (CNBC, 17 Sep 2026) shows damage extending across multiple pumping stations, consistent with a genuine multi-week repair job rather than a purely precautionary shutdown. No pipeline flow has actually resumed yet as of 20 Sep 2026, so mbd remains 0 pending a confirmed restart; Yanbu continues drawing on its estimated 5-7 day storage buffer plus Egypt's Ain Sukhna/Sidi Kerir reserves in the meantime. Escalation (18 Sep 2026): Bloomberg reports Aramco has told at least two European term-contract refiners they will receive zero crude deliveries in October — the first confirmed full month-long cutoff to term customers, going beyond the earlier 'some cargoes cancelled' reporting. Kpler separately estimates Petroline will run at only ~50% of normal capacity for up to six weeks, cutting Yanbu exports by roughly 2.5-2.7 mb/d over that period.
weekly_flows.source: Bloomberg (16 & 18 Sep 2026); CNBC (15 & 17 Sep 2026); Al Jazeera (14 & 17 Sep 2026); BOE Report (16 Sep 2026); Kpler (17 Sep 2026); OilPrice.com (19 Sep 2026)

weekly_flows.event_explanation: Venezuela's oil exports were almost unchanged in August 2026 at ~1.17 mb/d, with larger flows to India and Europe offsetting lower shipments to the US, per trade-flow data reported 1 Sep 2026. August crude production was ~1.145 mb/d, up from ~1.122 mb/d in July. Chevron's own lifting of Venezuelan crude eased slightly to ~286 kb/d in August from ~293 kb/d in July. Separately, on 2 Sep 2026 Chevron and Venezuela's interim government signed a $7bn investment accord targeting a roughly five-year path to ~600 kb/d of Chevron-operated production, versus ~280 kb/d currently — a structural expansion plan, not yet reflected in current flow.
weekly_flows.source: BOE Report (1 Sep 2026, trade-flow data); CNBC, The Hill (2 Sep 2026, Chevron-Venezuela accord)

weekly_flows.route: Ras Tanura / Ju'aymah Gulf loadings (Hormuz transit + Sohar, Oman ship-to-ship reroute)
weekly_flows.event_explanation: With Petroline shut (see flow #1 / disruption #6), Aramco is routing substantially more crude out through the Gulf via Hormuz and transshipping via ship-to-ship transfer off Sohar, Oman, to reach long-haul vessels without needing the Red Sea pipeline route. Vortexa's 28-day moving average of Hormuz-transit oil rose from ~1.2 mb/d (1 Sep) to ~1.9 mb/d (16 Sep); separately, maritime-intelligence firm Huax puts combined Ras Tanura + Ju'aymah loadings at ~4 mb/d. Reuters separately reports Aramco sold ~60 million barrels of crude for September-October loading via this Sohar STS route. These are three different measurements (transit MA, terminal loadings, contracted cargo volume) of the same underlying shift and should not be summed; treat each figure distinctly. This reroute is why oil markets have judged the Petroline outage 'less disruptive than feared' (CNBC, 18 Sep 2026) even though the pipeline itself remains shut.
weekly_flows.source: Bloomberg (16 Sep 2026, 'Saudis Pivot to Send More Oil Via Hormuz After Pipeline Shut'); AGBI (17 Sep 2026); Reuters via Investing.com (Sep 2026, Aramco Gulf export volumes); CNBC (18 Sep 2026)

disruptions.description: "2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis": US/Israel strikes on Iran (Operation Epic Fury, 28 Feb 2026) triggered Iranian closure of the strait, ship boardings and mining. Ceasefire (8 Apr) failed; US naval blockade of Iranian ports (13 Apr-29 May); further escalation 5-6 Sept 2026 (US struck 3 Iranian tankers, Iran fired missiles at US warships). Brent spiked to $126 in March, settled at $104.61 on 11 Sep 2026 (down 2.8% on the day, up 8.7% on the week). Saudi Arabia (-20%), Iraq (-70% at peak), Kuwait, Qatar, UAE and Iran all hit. Bypass routes (Saudi East-West/Yanbu, UAE Habshan-Fujairah, Iraq Kirkuk-Ceyhan) together carry only ~9 mb/d vs the ~20 mb/d the strait normally carries — and the Petroline bypass is now itself shut (disruption #6), pushing Saudi Arabia to route more crude back through Hormuz itself under naval escort rather than around it. Separately, Iran-backed Houthi forces completed capture of Yemen's Red Sea coastline and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait (11-13 Sep 2026, see disruption #7), opening a second major chokepoint front alongside Hormuz. The Persian Gulf Strait Authority (Iran-aligned) published an updated list on 14 Sep 2026 of vessels it deems in violation of its Hormuz protocols, threatening fines, detention or confiscation.
disruptions.source: Wikipedia: 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis; Al Jazeera (6-7 Sep, 11-13 Sep 2026); International Crisis Group (1 Sep 2026); Bloomberg (16 Sep 2026)

disruptions.description: Despite a Ukrainian drone strike on Novorossiysk port on 8 Apr 2026, Kazakhstan’s energy ministry confirmed CPC loadings continued normally. Ukraine agreed with the US (reported 8 Aug 2026) to refrain from targeting CPC-linked tankers specifically, reducing risk to this route relative to Russia’s own Baltic terminals. That tanker-specific truce does not cover the terminal's own infrastructure: a drone incident on 8 Sep 2026 affected SPM-2 and SPM-3 at the CPC marine terminal, prompting a brief loading pause; the Energy Ministry said on 9 Sep that inspections found no issues preventing further operations and no environmental impact, and loading resumed with Kazakh crude acceptance unaffected throughout. Separately, Kazakhstan's diversification push away from CPC dependency remains mostly talk so far — Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov backed Baku-Supsa as a possible alternative route on 25 Aug 2026 but said direct negotiations with Azerbaijan hadn't yet begun, and Azerbaijan's offer to take up to 2.2 million tonnes/year via BTC compares to KazMunayGas's own expectation of shipping only up to 1.6 million tonnes via BTC in 2026 — a small fraction of CPC's ~1.5-1.6 mb/d (roughly 75-80 million tonnes/year).
disruptions.source: Ukrainska Pravda (8 Aug 2026); Pipeline Technology Journal; The Times of Central Asia (attacks on CPC and Kazakhstan's oil exports, 21 Sep 2026); Kazakh Ministry of Energy statements (9 & 25 Aug/Sep 2026)

disruptions.description: Drone attack on 13 Sep 2026 hit the East-West Pipeline (Petroline) at multiple points near Riyadh and Medina, forcing a shutdown. Drones were traced to Maysan province, Iraq, launched by Iranian-aligned militants; Saudi Arabia subsequently removed the Maysan operations commander from his post in response. Petroline is Saudi Arabia's primary bypass route around the Strait of Hormuz (see disruption #1), carrying oil from the Eastern Province to the Red Sea export terminal at Yanbu — so this shutdown compounds the existing Hormuz crisis rather than offering relief from it, removing one of the few working bypass corridors. Satellite imagery reviewed by analysts (CNBC, 17 Sep 2026) shows damage across multiple pumping stations along the route, consistent with a genuine multi-week physical repair job rather than a purely precautionary shutdown. Saudi Arabia is instead absorbing much of the impact by pushing significantly more crude through the Gulf/Hormuz route itself, using US naval escort for short-haul transits and ship-to-ship transfers off Sohar, Oman, to reach long-haul vessels — Reuters reports ~60 million barrels sold for Sep-Oct loading via this route. Despite that workaround, Bloomberg (18 Sep 2026) reports Aramco has told at least two European refiners under term contracts they will get no crude at all in October — the clearest sign yet that some buyers cannot be made whole via the Hormuz/Sohar reroute alone, prompting customers like Poland's Orlen to scramble for North Sea, US and Kazakh replacement barrels (see tenders #1, cargo_substitution #4). Oil markets have nonetheless judged the overall outage 'less disruptive than feared' at the aggregate level (CNBC, 18 Sep 2026); Brent finished the week of 18 Sep roughly flat. On 19 Sep 2026, Yemen's Houthi forces claimed missile, cruise-missile and drone attacks on “sensitive sites” in Riyadh and on Aramco facilities in Yanbu — the Red Sea terminal city the East-West Pipeline feeds — the first such strike claimed on the Saudi capital since fighting resumed in Yemen. Saudi-led coalition forces said the attacks were intercepted/thwarted; Aramco did not confirm damage and the claims are unverified. No confirmed impact on the pipeline restart timeline, but it adds a new direct-attack risk to the Yanbu terminal itself on top of the pipeline shutdown.
disruptions.source: Bloomberg (16 & 18 Sep 2026); CNBC (15, 17 & 18 Sep 2026); Al Jazeera (14 & 17 Sep 2026); AGBI (17 Sep 2026); BOE Report (16 Sep 2026); Kpler (17 Sep 2026); OilPrice.com (19 Sep 2026); Wikipedia: 2026 East-West Crude Oil Pipeline attack; Times of Israel, Al Jazeera, NPR, Euronews, Irish Times (19-20 Sep 2026)

disruptions.location: Mocha and Mayyun (Perim) island, southern Red Sea, Yemen
disruptions.estimated_capacity_affected: ~12% of global trade transits this strait, including ~11% of maritime oil and ~8% of LNG
disruptions.actual_flow_affected: IMF PortWatch recorded 31 vessel transits through Bab al-Mandeb on 13 Sep 2026, vs 43 on the same date a year earlier (~28% down) — still-partial figure, not broken out by tanker-specific volumes; during 2023-2025 Houthi escalations, Red Sea shipping volumes fell 50-55% as major carriers rerouted via the Cape of Good Hope (adding 20+ transit days), so a deeper decline than the current ~28% is plausible if crude-specific rerouting follows the same pattern
disruptions.expected_restart: Not applicable — this is a territorial/military control change, not a temporary closure; no resolution timeline
disruptions.description: Iran-backed Houthi forces completed their takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coastline over the weekend of 11-13 Sep 2026, capturing the port city of Mocha and the strategic island of Mayyun (Perim), giving them effective control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait — the southern gateway to the Red Sea and Suez/SUMED route, roughly 20km from the African coast. This opens a second major chokepoint front alongside the ongoing Strait of Hormuz crisis (disruption #1). It raises risk to Red Sea-adjacent routes including Egypt's Suez/SUMED system and Israel's Ashkelon-Eilat pipeline (both still shown Green/Normal in this dashboard — no confirmed direct disruption to their throughput has been reported yet, but both are flagged as new watch items). Historically, Houthi control of this area has driven major container shipping lines to reroute around the Cape of Good Hope rather than test the strait, even after stated assurances of safe passage; whether this recurs for crude tankers specifically is not yet confirmed by public reporting. Escalating beyond the coastline/strait seizure, Houthi forces on 19 Sep 2026 also fired missiles and drones directly at Riyadh and claimed a separate strike on Aramco facilities in Yanbu (see disruption #6) — Saudi Arabia's first air-raid alert in the capital since fighting resumed in Yemen. Saudi coalition defences said the attacks were intercepted; no confirmed casualties or infrastructure damage. This marks the clearest sign yet that the Houthi threat is extending from chokepoint control toward direct attacks on Saudi mainland oil infrastructure.
disruptions.source: Al Jazeera (11 & 13 Sep 2026); NBC News (13 Sep 2026); NPR (11-12 Sep 2026); Times of Israel (12 Sep 2026); Euronews (12 Sep 2026); Times of Israel, Al Jazeera, NPR, Euronews, Irish Times, Manila Times (19-20 Sep 2026)

disruptions.location: Hamada and Tahara oilfields and a pumping station (Western Libya); Wafa, Al-Khamsa, El Feel and Sharara threatened
disruptions.event_type: Security-force pipeline valve closure / labour dispute
disruptions.estimated_capacity_affected: Hamada and Tahara fields plus a pumping station fully halted; Wafa, Al-Khamsa and El Feel put on a one-week partial cut from 15 Sep; Sharara (Libya's largest field, historically ~300 kb/d) named as one of seven fields facing complete closure if the dispute isn't resolved — no official combined bpd figure disclosed
disruptions.actual_flow_affected: Not quantified by NOC or wire sources yet; Libya's national output (~1.4-1.5 mb/d per July 2026 NOC reporting, see weekly_flows #8) not yet confirmed reduced
disruptions.expected_restart: Petroleum Facilities Guard set a one-week partial-cut window from 15 Sep 2026 (i.e. to ~22 Sep), threatening a full shutdown of seven fields after that if demands aren't met; no resolution confirmed as of 21 Sep 2026
disruptions.status: Ongoing — partial cuts in effect, full shutdown of additional fields threatened
disruptions.description: Members of Libya's Petroleum Facilities Guard (PFG), a state-affiliated security force currently under the Defense Ministry, closed a valve on the main Hamada-Zawiya crude pipeline on 15 Sep 2026, halting production completely at the Hamada and Tahara oilfields and a pumping station. NOC called the closure illegal and said it may declare force majeure if the valve stays shut or if other fields see similar forced shutdowns; as of the latest reporting no force majeure had actually been declared. The PFG is demanding to be transferred financially and administratively from the Defense Ministry to NOC, with a set timetable for the move, and announced a one-week partial production cut at Wafa, Al-Khamsa and El Feel starting 15 Sep, threatening complete closure of these plus other fields (reporting names seven fields total including Sharara) if its demands aren't met within that week. This is a recurring pattern of PFG/local-group leverage over Libyan oil infrastructure (echoes 2019/2024 Sharara shutdowns) rather than a new type of risk, but it lands directly on Libya's Zawiya/Mellitah export route (weekly_flows #8, infrastructure #33) at a moment when global buyers are already scrambling for non-Gulf/non-Russian barrels (see tenders #3-6, cargo_substitution #4).
disruptions.source: OilPrice.com (15 Sep 2026); Arab News (15 Sep 2026); The Media Line (15 Sep 2026); Libya Herald (16 Sep 2026); Daily Sabah (15 Sep 2026); Energy Intelligence (15 Sep 2026)
